title: Jeremiah laments captivity; the soul under hostile powers; release to captives
english: Jeremiah, after his people had been taken captive and were dwelling in Babylon, laments the city, the land, and the people in light of the events that have befallen them. He mourns particular sections and divisions, tracing them in writing, beginning with the elementary elements as known among the Hebrews, and proceeding sequentially. After composing a lament for each of these elements individually, and then a lament over all things beginning with the letter Tau—which is the final letter of the Hebrew alphabet—he returns to Aleph and laments again. He repeats this process four times, going through the twenty-two elements of the Hebrew alphabet.

If we observe the soul becoming subject to the devil, or even to his angels, and simply yielding to the hostile powers, thereby losing the capacity for intellectual contemplation and the ability to perceive and understand being, we shall in some way comprehend the nature of captivity and the one who has taken captive. Yet, by fleeing to Christ, who proclaimed, according to the prophet Isaiah, “Release to the captives,” we shall be set free from captivity, even if the captor manages to bind us before liberation arrives. For Jesus came “to bring out those bound in chains, and those sitting in darkness in the house of prison.”

Therefore, the Hebrews say that the books of the ancient Scripture correspond in number to the elements, so as to constitute a complete introduction to the knowledge of God, just as the elements serve as an introduction to wisdom for all who learn. And for this reason, the number is quadrupled, perhaps because the elements of the body are four in number. Shortly thereafter: The edition of Aquila and Theodotion is not found among the Lamentations; only that of Symmachus and the Seventy is present. Again: One might inquire how, given that the superscription of the book is plural—“Lamentations”—the singular “Lamentation” appears in the prologue. But some manuscripts have multiple readings, divided according to the elements, while all are ultimately brought back to one, toward a single hypothesis: Israel, as they are recalled.

Blessed is the tear shed from love, for the holy one says, “Weep with those who weep.” As the Lord drew near to Jerusalem, he wept and said: “If you, even you, had only known on this day what would bring you peace.”

Jerusalem, Jerusalem, you who kill the prophets and stone those sent to you—how often I have longed to gather your children together, as a hen gathers her chicks under her wings, and you were not willing. Now if “blessed are those who weep, for they shall laugh,” then it was fitting that Jeremiah, this mystic one, should weep a weeping of mourning and, according to “blessed are those who mourn,” should mourn those worthy of mourning. It seems, however, that the multitude of the people, insofar as it is spoken of, denotes the Israelites dwelling there, while the multitude of the nations, as we have said before, denotes the proselytes. For the purpose of uplift, since the theoretical things are more akin to the soul and more constant than the practical, the multitude of the people might signify the wealth of the doctrines of the blessed Jerusalem, and the multitude of the nations the great number of good works. And shortly after: The people, filled alone, sits; the bride, having cast away the bridegroom’s word, becomes like a widow who once multiplied among the aforesaid nations. As far as the words go, it is fitting to understand Jerusalem as being spoken of with wonder, due to her change toward the more grim, having sat down remembering the people who once were numerous, so that her solitude and desolation might be hers—having once had a husband, the vivifying preserver, when she followed him present and helping, and now being deserted and forsaken by him on account of her sins. And furthermore: These things, then, pertain to the literal sense; but for the intellectual sense, Jerusalem, enriching herself and multiplying among peoples and nations and ruling over regions, is the divine soul. And it is not marvelous, if not only a house, nor even a homestead, nor even this village, if it were called such, nor even the city that possesses such things, but rather Jerusalem, surpassing all cities and honored by God, is named the perfect soul—of a magnitude worthy of a great city, by the greatest surrounding that envelops it from

title: How the captivity of the contemplative soul is undone in Christ
english: Sophia and every virtue, when multiplied and being built up, produce manifold structures. And after a little while: just as one can see Jerusalem nourished, increasing in people and nations and ruling over lands, so too, if virtue is subject to change, it once was solitary, then widowed and enslaved, so that it must even pay tribute to the enemy who has seized it, according to the soul of the one who has fallen from the truth. What then need be said also about the fact that, having begun to rule over regions, it is enslaved by its enemies to such an extent that it continually pays tribute, serving cruel masters who command nothing good; and perhaps for each of its failures in this place, it pays a certain tribute to Nebuchadnezzar, who is interpreted as "Enclosure" and "knowledge of distress"; not only to Nebuchadnezzar, but also to his satraps. Upon the first Lament, beginning with Aleph, we have preserved the word. As for this, what could one say, when it is said that the city wept in the night, so that its tears were upon its cheeks? Unless, indeed, one says that the inhabitants of the city, mourning, are those who also pay tribute, having been reminded of the peace and liberty from which they have come into such slavery and humiliation. How then shall we recount the night-weeping, or that in the time of rest for all mankind, the city, remembering its sorrows—namely, those who dwell in the city do not rest, but weep, and weep with heads covered, as the tears flow upon their cheeks? Moreover, the lamentation especially intensified upon them, and the tears overflowed,

Not even one comforter existing to console them from among so many who loved them, and every lover rejecting their friendship and turning it into enmity—who then, as regards the wording, were the lovers of her formerly, from whom not one comforter existed to console her? Perhaps the other cities of Judea, therefore possibly loving the metropolis, did not call upon her in time of distress. And shortly after: These things, then, concerning the literal sense. But if the word, as we have set forth in the preceding passages, Jerusalem signifies the affectionate soul, then this soul would be said to weep, having been cast out from its native dwelling, become confused in disposition, and holding a state contrary to laughter—the laughter that comes from joy and cheerfulness, which our Lord promises will exist for those who mourn, saying: “Blessed are those who weep now, for they shall laugh.” And in the Book of Job it is said: “My mouth is filled with true laughter.” Perhaps for this reason also one of the patriarchs is named Laughter. Therefore, the one who groans because he is in the tabernacle, as the Apostle has declared, saying: “For indeed we who are in the tabernacle groan, being burdened,” longs for the laughter promised in the promise and the divine cheerfulness, and weeps a nourishing and beneficial weeping for the soul. We suppose, then, that to love is more divine and, so to speak, spiritual, whereas to be fond is bodily and more human. Yet perhaps, regarding those who are better, it is to be observed that no one who loves poorly exists to comfort her from among all those who love her.

As for the lesser ones: all who loved her betrayed her, becoming to her enemies. For the more humble among them not only betrayed her but also became her enemies; while the more distinguished merely refrained from offering comfort. This is how one might understand the literal sense: Judah exchanged her own place, these reasons having come upon her—her humiliation, which she brought upon herself by sinning, losing the standing and the exaltation she once possessed in piety, having abandoned it—and furthermore, her extensive servitude, to which she had subjected herself, enslaved to her passions. Having been transplanted among the nations, she was settled, yet found no rest there; all her enemies, who pursued, seized, and prevailed over her, having made her dwell among the nations who oppressed her. This is the understanding of the literal sense: when the law declares, "Three times each year every male of yours shall appear before the Lord your God," the people, after the temple had been rebuilt in Zion from the time of Solomon, eagerly undertook to observe the prescribed festival. title: Alphabet threne structure and the turn from letter to spirit
english: In those times when great joy and cheerfulness were among them, they hastened to the feast, gathering Jews from every place to Mount Zion. Many of the gates, which had been built in Zion from all the regions, the word says, have been utterly destroyed; and the priests are groaning, clearly because they are unable to perform the priestly duties prescribed for the feasts and the other days—either because they have been led into captivity, or because there is no one coming to them who seeks their priestly services and demands their ministrations. Moreover, the virgins of Zion, it is said, are being led away, and it is evident that they are taken by the victorious enemies. As for reflection: of Zion, called the contemplative and theorizing power, there are many ways of the diverse doctrines, mystical and physical and ethical, and perhaps also logical, which lead to the understanding and contemplation of the things set before us. Therefore, when one, having lost the disciplined practice of these things, becomes confused, all these ways wander without being traveled, though a festival exists along the previously mentioned ways, when they are walked, examined, and, as I might say, tread upon in order; but they mourn when they are deserted, neither inquiring nor passing through, because those who walk have fallen away and been taken captive by the passions, dragged about toward worse things. Zion, possessing nothing sweet anywhere, endures bitterness by itself. One must not take the present bitterness as being upon some kind of anger. The clarity of the word is such as this: they wished to afflict, or were afflicting, the Jewish land before the times of the captivity.

But they did not prevail, even while God was defending the Jews, when they offered themselves as worthy helpers. Yet when they sinned and, in addition to not listening to the prophets, even killed them—the sons of Israel—then they were handed over, helpless, to those who oppressed them, so that their enemies became their heads, as Symmachus has declared, rulers. Others, perhaps, who were enemies while living among the oppressors, either by invention or by substance, prospered in prosperity, having become subject to those who oppress, namely, those who remain behind due to their sins, whom the Lord has humbled because of the multitude of their godless deeds, even those who have transgressed and done this to such an extent that not even mercy is left for their infants, but they are led away into captivity, driven by every oppressor. Beginning with those who started and rejoiced in the Lord’s handing them over to humility because of the abundance of their godless deeds—those who had made covenants with the holy oracles toward Him but did not keep them. The power of these words must be made clear to us: they examine who is the daughter of Zion, and in what she possesses her beauty; what is the pasture, which the rulers of the daughter of Zion do not possess, like sheep owners bewildered about grazing; and how these, deprived of strength, go forward against the face of the one who pursues. But we consider that the mountain of Zion is indeed the mother of the assembly within her, the daughter called Zion; and the beauty of the daughter of Zion is her possession, the garments she wears, which possession, taken in the time of pasturing, was seized by the enemies and went forth from them.

Of these, the world was, that is, it was carried off (for this is a more emphatic way of saying it went out), and the leaders of the synagogue, because the enemies pressed upon them and took them captive, being at a loss for their kin, could not find nourishment like sheep. Just as rams, driven and not fed, go weakly forward, yielding to the force of those pursuing them, so also the leaders, having become captives, being led away into the land of those who took them captive, went forward not in strength, in appearance to the pursuer. But for understanding, such a soul is the daughter of Zion; just as the daughter of righteousness is the righteous one, and the daughter of wisdom is the wise one, so (since Zion is the place of observation) the observant and theoretically investigating daughter might be called Zion. What, then, could I rightly consider as her beauty and worth, except the wealth of the holy doctrines of truth, examined together with wisdom? Therefore, when someone neglects, after having attained beauty and worth, both the continuity of these things and the increase of the divine wealth, the things that as yet the world has attained flow out and depart. title: Captivity, bonds, and the freedom proclaimed to prisoners
english: Drink. For this reason, having grown weak and been overtaken by the pursuer—who is “our adversary, the devil”—they go before him, being driven wherever he wishes to lead them. But if the aforementioned daughter Zion attends to her beauty and loveliness and takes care to guard her dignity, she scorns and sneers at the king of the Assyrians, as we have learned from Isaiah saying: “You have been made worthless and you have been mocked, virgin daughter Zion.” For the one who remembers suffering something in these present circumstances does not recall the present hardship, but the past. And shortly after: Having pondered these things in that place and seeking a reminder of her former lowliness and her removals, because her people have fallen into the hands of an oppressor and the events that have befallen her have occurred, we consider whether perhaps the proper lowliness is not something other than sin, just as exaltation is right action, and removal is not the doing of anyone except through wicked conduct—for this is sufficient to drive away from God and from all that is naturally most beautiful. Therefore, when Jerusalem, that is, its inhabitants, drunk and having turned away from sin, was brought low, she was not noticed in her stumblings; but when her repayments came, because her people had fallen into the hands of the oppressor, with no one helping her, then she remembered the causes of her suffering, recognizing them as the reasons why her people had fallen and why she herself had been left helpless.

And after a little while: But if the soul of such a kind is Jerusalem, it is worthy to seek her people, whose falling into the hands of the oppressor, when there is no helper present, she remembers the humility of her own people, and still also her own whom she has driven away in expulsions; and besides these, her desires which were from ancient days. See whether the doctrines in the scientific soul are not the people of Jerusalem, whoever, through neglect and carelessness having happened to the soul, falls prostrate under every oppressor. For the doctrines of the negligent flow away, crushed by the powers of the land of sins beside the neglectful of the better, not having at all the help from the word. The meaning of the word is such. Since Jerusalem has sinned, she has become in confusion and tumult to such an extent that all who formerly praised her have changed, desiring to destroy such a city, having seen her shameful conduct. But she herself, having suffered these things because of her sins, has fallen into confusion and dishonor from those who once praised her, groaning no longer to come forward from her sins, but having diminished them, has withdrawn backward. And after a little while: But if Jerusalem is called such a soul, she is anxious and perceptive and “understanding the peace of God which surpasses all mind,” for it is possible through many causes to sin in this way, thus it is shown that she has fallen into confusion, having departed from the good things and having become in the worse things.

Anyone who has fallen from virtue and now lives in fellowship with wickedness is said to enjoy sound health in the midst of filth. This indicates the cessation of Jerusalem’s sins—not the sins that were once stretching forward, nor those being committed in the pasture of transgressions, but rather the sins that are turning backward upon their own proper good. According to the bodily narrative, the statement concerning Jerusalem now is this: the uncleanness of Jerusalem is an impediment; but what it is an impediment to, the prophet has left for us to perceive. Perhaps it indicates that uncleanness is hindering her journey. Yet, being such, it also indicates that Jerusalem has not remembered her latter end. The one who has this before his eyes and sees what will be repaid because of the sins will not sin. Therefore, on account of this uncleanness as an impediment to her, and because she does not remember her latter end—her wonderful and great things, which she possessed when she was worthy of being inspected—she has been brought down and brought into lowliness, formerly being exalted and greater than all praise. Moreover, after all this, there was no one consoling her who had brought down her greatest things. Upon these things, consider my humiliation, Lord, because my enemy is magnified over the things that have happened to my homeland. title: Impurity blocking the holy way; first thoughts of the Threne
english: It may be possible to encounter impurity in someone who is not the cause of it. Let us also consider the first thoughts of the lament. A soul of such a kind, having fallen away, is necessarily in impurity, and this impurity prevents one from walking the holy path. Just as God commanded Moses the holy man and his successor Jesus to remove their sandals when treading upon holy ground—so that one would not carry dead skin upon the feet into the sacred place—so too, if someone wishes to walk unhindered, they ought not only to remove their sandals but also to wash away the impurity that has come from the dust around the feet. And we may regard this as a symbol: the Savior pouring water into the basin and washing the feet of the disciples, saying to Peter, who did not yet understand the mystery and therefore resisted: "If I do not wash you, you have no share with me," and "What I am doing, you do not understand now, but you will understand afterward." Therefore, we must gather around, as it were, the feet of the soul, cleanse them of impurity, and pray to Jesus that he may wash them, so that we may be able to have a share with him. For if this impurity remains, it is an obstacle to our walking the way according to sound reason—the way of which the Savior said, "I am the way." Indeed, it is evident that the healthy soul, or even one that wishes to be such, does not merely focus on the present but looks ahead to what it will encounter in the future from the things being accomplished. And if one considers something good in the present to be occurring, they foresee the bitter thing that will be in the future, and thus send away what seems pleasant, doing the opposite, in order not to fall later into some hardship. But if one encounters something painful in the present, good hopes take over the apparent harshness, and willingly subjects itself to the roughness of what may seem terrible to some, in order to attain the sweet things reserved for those who endure these things.

All these things, he says, the Jerusalem which is called more truly so, suffering, could not even find comfort in the one offering consolation; for, having turned away from the word within her and become wholly given over to passion, she lost her helper, the one who continually arms himself against pains and against the dreaded things deemed so, and the disposition she had toward him. Moreover, upon these things, behold my humiliation as a citizen—so that a relative of the soul might speak it—my citizen’s sorrow, through which I was taught philanthropy, is my own misfortune. Consider then, O Lord, and do not utterly abandon her who has suffered the aforementioned things; do not overlook her enemy, that is, wickedness magnified and poured out against her. For the words “look, O Lord, upon my humiliation” may be understood tropically as referring to the word dwelling within the soul, having been dishonored and humbled, and, to speak plainly, to her own royal estate having been lost.

The desires of Jerusalem, therefore, are to be understood as the things in the temple, and the holy things of the holies kept for the priestly ministry, properly ordered, and likewise the things otherwise destined to be kept in the temple, which are believed to be divine, such as the golden lampstand and the rest. For the people, having trusted these things to be stored in the temple for God’s glory, preferred above all to suffer something themselves at the hands of the enemies rather than see these things fall into hostile hands. And it is customary for those who are circumcised to call the temple holy.

Moreover, something most paradoxical has befallen Jerusalem in the time of her captivity: she saw nations, whom God had commanded not to enter the church, trampling the holy place, where even the Israelites were not permitted to enter, except only the priests who had been deemed worthy, together with those not chosen for purification, to become holy in that place. And the enemies advanced even as far as the forbidden zones, entering that spot which the high priest alone could enter, with great purification, once a year. And shortly thereafter—

title: Unless I wash you: cleansing and share with Christ
english: We have set forth the proposition that when a soul of this kind happens to be encountered, it is necessary to recognize the natural good things belonging to it as a cosmos in its own right, through which it was healed by the divine, stored up in its inaccessible parts for everything except the word of the high priest, and called its desires. Moreover, upon all these things, the enemy who has gained mastery in the ancient contest, having afflicted the soul that wages war not well for itself but rather has been left behind worthily by divine aid, extends himself through the power of his activity into evil things, drags away the ruling faculty and leaves the soul that has departed from God desolate of good things. And the nations, according to the place, are to be understood allegorically as the crowd of vices that have entered into the formed ruling faculty, so as to be a receptacle and true sanctification of God for the pure mind wishing to rest again. These nations God utterly forbids from entering the church; for what else could we consider more forbidden by God from entering into a soul numbered in the church of God than the works and the mind of the flesh, which are truly nations hostile to God? For "the flesh wars against the spirit," "the mind of the flesh is enmity toward God"; "for to the law of God it is not subject, nor indeed can it be." They groaned because of famine and because of little food, the soul turning back and leaving behind provided the most precious things. But how did the previously mentioned desires, taken away by the enemies, provide for the purchase of food? Yet "the enemy stretched forth his hand against all things," and having been satisfied with taking what he wished, he left the rest behind, in exchange for which they bought food.

Jerusalem prays, Lord, look upon my shame, since you have destroyed the world by famine. Perhaps different desires preceded, first the foretold things which the enemy had stretched out his hand upon, secondly each person's own desires from among the people; and the common things were taken, but instead of the particular things, each one bought food for himself. Moreover, for guidance, just as Esau sold his birthright for red stew, of which he became surnamed (Edom meaning Red Earth; and indeed he became earthly, having despised the birthrights, having made earthly things which Jacob, as necessary, transferred to him in a second discourse because he happened to be in a body), so also Jerusalem. But the one who gives Jacob the worthy to obtain, which things he had desired, even if he did not previously choose them; but the people of Jerusalem have given indeed also themselves because of food, but not having sanctified this construction, but the Babylonians who were about to insult the given desires. For Jacob knows how to adorn the things from Esau, but the Babylonians do not use the given things for their own good. And so the soul, through lack of necessities, rejects the divine teachings to those who, out of curiosity, desire to learn for slander and mockery. 30 He has shown the one upon the conflagration of the strongest buildings touching or the fall of the superior ones in it of the city, to the soul and to those outside as if burning with the calamities. He also indicates the conception of those who have been subdued into slavery like in a field with nets,

Those who did not make good use of freedom. For these, "not stretching forward to the things that are ahead, but forgetting the things that are behind," they turned away from glory into dishonor, from freedom into slavery, and have become instead of honorable ones, darkened and obscure through dishonor and insolence; because of these things the city has fallen into endless grief. 31 Providence, he says, has not slept over my impious deeds; for God, as if taking them into his hands, has intertwined them through examination with the works of recompense. And these things have become to me like a yoke placed upon the neck and slavery imposed upon it; for just as I served slavery to Nebuchadnezzar, my sins are slavery, therefore I have become weak, delivered over to these things whose dominion I cannot withstand. And shortly after: His yoke upon my neck is shown. But it is indicated through the present expression that the things spoken of as concerning our passions ought to be taken more tropically in regard to God. For how otherwise could the impieties of Jerusalem be understood, joined to the hand of God, except tropically? For no one could speak these things literally. And how is it not absurd, that while the city of Jerusalem is said to lift up its neck tropically, the things spoken as concerning God do not hear the same manner? title: Defilement, washings, and the path back to holiness
english:
The sins that have weakened me, having cast me away from the divine oversight and delivered me into the service of the sovereign of evils, are such that, due to the boundless and infinite nature of wickedness, I cannot fully minister to her nor satisfy her with sufficient provision. Indeed, sin truly humbles and presses down upon one, causing the gaze to fall low; yet the yoke and the ever-present, piercing conscience continually sting and urge one not to relent, stripping away all boldness. Moreover, as he says, permission and the strength with which I did not act well have been granted, and I behold the evils that hold me dissolving.  
He did not take them from my midst (for even if I had been deprived of them, I could have used them elsewhere), but in my midst he judged them guilty for the very acts of impiety I committed. My chosen ones have endured the most severe trials, having drunk the wine of the Lord’s wrath, which He trod in the winepress until it filled me and the virgin daughter of the most royal Judah. One might say that the strong are those who wage war and defend the fatherland, while the elect are the noble or the wise. He clarifies the winepress by referencing what was said in the Psalms concerning the punishment of sinners: “A cup in the hand of the Lord, full of unmixed wine, mingled with spice,” pouring from the one being punished upon the one being punished, until all the sinners of the earth drink, while the remnants of the vintage remain for the lesser sinners still existing, to whom finally “the one who treads the winepress” shall be emptied.  
It is not difficult to see how the Lord trod the winepress upon the virgin daughter of Judah.

For indeed, as the proverb says, “Each one reaps what he sows,” and so too, perhaps, each one harvests what he cultivates. The one who produces superior wine will rejoice in the fruits of his own labor. But the one who cultivates “the vineyard of Sodom and the vine-dressing of Gomorrah, bearing fruit for the tribe of bitterness, yielding a cluster of gall and a wrath that shields cannot withstand—all of which the Lord gathers together”—into a single winepress, where his evil deeds are trodden underfoot and crushed, such a person, in keeping with such fruits, drinks in order to vomit up the gall, the bitterness, and the wrath. And he drinks, according to Jeremiah, to purge himself; according to Isaiah, to awaken and clothe himself in kindred glory. For the Lord does not tread the winepress in vain, and especially not for the virgin daughter of Judah. 34 Thus, the soul, having received many gifts from its Creator—both natural and chosen—yet deprived of them through wickedness and suffering punishment, acknowledges what it has endured. And the one called to be broken in the time of retribution is the moment when, according to Ezekiel, “none of the righteous deeds which the righteous one has done shall be remembered in the day of his sin.” Mourning what has befallen her, she is benefited, for to those who mourn and weep belongs the promise of consolation and laughter. 35 She declared that the cause of her lamentations was the absence of the one who turns back her soul—namely, the one who restores it according to Symmachus. And she says that her sons have perished through the strengthening of the enemy, by means of which they were exiled; for although we are pious, we do not prevail, for the weak, as they progress, are destroyed and utterly broken beneath the feet—“becoming thin as dust before the face of the wind,”

And as clay in the streets, becoming thin. For in proportion as we sin, it is nourished and gains strength; but when transgressions cease, it is, as it were, destroyed by famine. And from the opposing forces, the divine powers, when we act well, we strengthen ourselves and pursue those who sin. Therefore Symmachus, instead of "the obliterated ones," delivered "deserts." One might say these things of a contemplative soul that has attained the word of true divinity and, through slackness, has lost this joyful word and all its fruits, which it names as its children, because it has been strengthened against the evil that opposes it. Zion says the mountain, and the people of Jacob, and the mother-city Jerusalem. And God commanded Jacob with commandments by which, when transgressed, he was encircled by enemies; and according to Symmachus and another edition of the Seventy, the Lord commanded that those who oppress him should be round about him, namely, the powers appointed to do evil. The uncleanness of Jerusalem through sin, as through a sewer, he has shown. And in the midst, he speaks either of Zion and Jacob, or of the whole mountain as middle (for in part it is built upon), and of the whole people; now this signifies Jacob, the twelve scepters. And according to the word, it is possible to take Zion and Jerusalem in two ways: either the places or the inhabitants. But if Zion is a place, her hands are her works, for example.

title: Purity restored and the soul share with the Word
english: Agriculture and any handiwork, he says, are left spread out and not gathered together, failing to perform the proper work with their hands, as if in an idle and desolate land. If, however, he is speaking of those dwelling within, the hands would be farmers and laborers, not withdrawing their hands from work due to surrounding circumstances. But if the hands of Zion are being counted, how much more the members according to Scripture of God are to be regarded. And indeed, the mountain itself, as it were, groans with the people, lacking comfort from God or from a holy man. The mouth of the Lord must be heeded in the prophets, of whom Isaiah, who exists, declared: "For the mouth of the Lord has spoken these things." Yet Jerusalem, rewarded by the Savior as "having slain the prophets," moreover, provoked the mouth of the Lord to bitter pains by delivering them over. But the God who "seeks the blood of the prophets" delivers her to afflictions from wars and again to captivities, handing over her young men and virgins. Therefore, for what she has suffered, she confesses before others, presenting herself as an example to these, so that those who have learned God’s righteousness may not suffer similar things. After the perceptible, interpret virgins as those living in incorruptibility, and young men as those prospering in virtue. For often the holy ones also suffer with those responsible. The lovers, namely those who are such, Ezekiel has declared to Jerusalem, whom he calls Olivet, saying: "Thus says the Lord Lord: Behold, I will stir up your lovers against you from every side, sons of Babylon and all the Chaldeans." For these, though formerly friends by divine providence, have turned into enemies.

It often happens, under the impulse of love, that one turns into hatred; for he speaks concerning Samaria thus: “And Oholah played the harlot away from me, and she set herself upon her lovers, the Assyrians”; and shortly after: “Therefore he delivered her into the hands of her lovers, into the hands of the sons of Assyria.” He also speaks concerning Jerusalem: “And her sister Oholibah saw it, and she defiled her illicit affection more than the harlotry of her sister, and she set herself upon the sons of the Assyrians.” 41 In the prophecy, indeed, the soul grieves as if being persuaded of obvious things; but in the present Lamentation, as though these things have already come to pass, she grieves bitterly and, through sin, confesses that she has brought upon herself the utmost bitterness of God’s goodness, as if she, who was abundantly fruitful, had been made barren, and as if the most terrible thing—war by hostile hand—had befallen her. Since personification is employed, one should not seek a literal city whose womb bore children and whose heart was loosened. 42 He divides the word into eight parts, addressing Jerusalem toward her enemies, whom he wishes to hear, and toward God. But what does he urge upon the enemies for their hearing? And what does he say to God about them, as if they had rejoiced? Perhaps, therefore (since “her transgression and Israel’s transgression have become the instruction of the nations to provoke them to jealousy,” and “when the fullness of the nations has entered in, then all Israel will be saved”), he speaks prophetically first to those from the nations, and then to God concerning the second matters: “You were left behind to suffer so that you might take possession of the land, and I have become, through you, an enemy of God, though according to the election, beloved for the sake of the fathers, I continue to exist.”

Therefore, you have heard my lamentation and perceived its cause; for I am entirely consumed on account of your salvation, left bereft, lacking the one who continually comforts me amid the trials of evil. Now the "leader has departed from Judah, and he who was reckoned from his loins" has come—He to whom belonged "the things stored up," "the expectation of the nations"—at whose blood’s vengeance, no one remains to console Jerusalem. This means: let not their wickedness be allowed to persist unchecked; rather, may it be granted to you in oversight, as if one were to pray for wounds to come before a physician, in order to attain complete healing. For this is the whole: blessed above all is the one who does not sin, and second, blessed is the one whom God examines wholly for wickedness. Moreover, glean after the vintage the small remnants of the grape clusters left behind, as the poor do. Just as when you carefully inspected my vines, you cleansed them, removing every worthless shoot down to the tiniest bits—“the cluster of gall and the bunch of bitterness”—so too, let me glean after my enemies. This would be beneficial to me, for if they were fully saved alongside me, then I, according to your judgment, O Lord, would obtain salvation’s verdict; whom I see, I am deeply grieved and condemn myself, the oversight I need from you. Likewise, as David said: “He will utterly crush all the horns of the sinners.” Now he speaks of the rulers, in whom resides the strength of the nation…

title: Horns of power, pride of the ruling mind, and kingdoms as horns
english: Just as in the horned beasts, and because the body is laid bare, as the subjects are stripped by their rulers; and Daniel, too, represented the kingdoms by horns. Moreover, the horn signifies the arrogance of the ruling power, as in the saying: “Do not lift up your horn on high.” Having turned away his saving hand from them to the enemies, he made them vulnerable; and these, indeed, he called those who consume all things with flame. One might also say that any thought that excels is a horn, and fire is the “passions of disgrace,” to which the transgressor surrenders, having destroyed every surrounding help, according to the word: “The angel of the Lord shall encamp around those who fear him.” For indeed, in the temple, the enemies dared to commit slaughter, while God was consenting. And well is it said that he acts as an enemy; for God does not punish out of hostility, but wishing to benefit either those who suffer or those who observe. He also calls the temple a tent, according to its original sanctification, and the bow, the punitive power, as in Habakkuk: “You have bent your bow, you have made ready your arrows against the scepters, says the Lord,” clearly referring to the opposing powers and authorities. But the Son, who exists at the right hand of God and as Father, has zealously contended, overthrowing and destroying whatever they had set up as idols in God’s temple (for these are the lust of the eyes), and slaying the demons who had taken their place instead of the idols. He says that burdens are laid upon the houses, which Symmachus had granted as kingdoms. He takes up again the laments, as if one, grieving in mourning, were wandering about. Again he shows how a humble reason and a humble conception have been taken up, after the demolition of dwellings and fortifications, just as those who filled the ruling power. For virtues are indeed the dwellings, for by them we are sheltered; but fortifications are the unyielding reasonings. For this dismantling is not now “the lifting up of high things, those who exalt themselves against the knowledge of God,” nor is humility, by which one “learns the ordinances of God,” for these things are worthy of joy, not of lamentation. The tent, then, is the temple,

And he speaks of a vineyard and a vineyard when referring to Israel, according to the passage in David: “I brought a vine out of Egypt,” and in Isaiah: “The vineyard of my beloved became a wasteland.” And David adds: “Why have you broken down its wall?” and continues with the following words. But Isaiah says: “You have removed its hedge,” and then proceeds with what follows. These things the present Lamentation has also made clear. For having withdrawn his protection, God delivered Israel into the hands of its enemies, no longer encamping angels around it as guardians, because they did not fear God. Moreover, he abolished the appointed times for worship according to the law, as Isaiah declares: “My soul hates your fasts, your Sabbaths, and your appointed feasts.” This he called forgetfulness, yet not as a mere human passion. He also provoked the king and the priests, who, though they were portions of God, became indignant when they saw such things done by the impious, and they stood against them. He gave over the sacred vessels for liturgical use, no longer accepting the sacrifices of the wicked as pleasing, in accordance with the word: “I do not desire burnt offerings of rams, nor the fat of lambs, nor the blood of bulls and goats.” He also gave over the continuous wall of the city—the houses of the polis, that is, the royal palace—just as Symmachus had formerly delivered it. The enemies, having taken these things and the temple as if upon a complete victory, now celebrated with cries of wailing. But the rational soul within us is a spiritual altar, by means of which the passions are slain in sacrifice. For she has utterly removed all her safety, extending the measure of punishment; and this too Zechariah has beheld. And she mourns the wall and the outwork, which are worthy of lamentation, the causes of weeping and of becoming guilty before those who see—“Who can scatter the counsel of the Lord? And who can turn back his high hand?” according to the blessed Isaiah. And whether it be a city or a soul that thus mourns, it is fitting that it become a trampling underfoot for the enemies, and that the angels who once guarded it on other grounds—those who were once with her and now are subject—should mourn for her. For if they rejoice over those who are saved, how could they not mourn over those who have fallen? As if one were beneath the earth or—

title: Do not lift your horn: arrogance judged and brought low
english: The sea has swallowed them, and they have become nothing. The king and the rulers, the false prophets, and even their law have been destroyed—compelled into slavery by necessity, though they had freely chosen and, even before their capture, had dissolved it. The gates of the soul are the senses; when the soul sins, these senses are overwhelmed by passions and become earthly. And the powers that guard these senses within the soul are dissolved when the mind, which once ruled, is lost, and the governing reasonings are overwhelmed in the passions. At that moment, the law and order of the soul perish, and it becomes Babylon, full of confusion, possessing nothing of divine providence to aid it.

It mournfully recounts the sights seen in the place of joy, now made so: for fear, they did not even allow the elders to lament, and they prepared the first virgins to see the earth, lest, appearing beautiful, they be seized by force from the very beauty in which they once excelled, and be dragged away. One might also say that those who long ago served in virtue, by which they were so named, have become like crowds, having implanted irrational passions within themselves according to reason, yet still doing nothing, and having expelled the guiding spirit within them, along with the worthy mourning they once possessed, having made themselves temperate and corrupted their reasonings—those very reasonings which once preserved them incorruptible.

The prophet says of his own opinion that it is the temple of God and the piety of the fatherland. As for the infants, their dissolution was brought about by famine. But if one looks higher, as one relates to kin by flesh, and considers the saying, “Who is weak, and I am not weak?”—then taking upon oneself their weak feelings, there arises a marring of true knowledge and a wandering instability of reason toward earthly things, and a deprivation of the opinion that lifts the head, according to the words, “But you,”

Lord, You are my defender, my glory, and the One who lifts up my head. He fully revealed wickedness, showing that there is no virtue in rebellion, nor any similarity in the one who transgresses. For what likeness is there between sin and being far from God, then drawing near and yet becoming estranged? For He says, “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have sin.” Therefore, “I will be sanctified among those who come near Me.” Because “the one who does not know the will of the Lord and does not do it will be beaten with few stripes, but the one who knows and does not do it will be beaten with many.” Thus, this suffering, which the prophets could not heal, requires only God. For this reason He took on flesh, as the prophets confessed their weakness, saying, “Lord, who has believed our report?” He also formerly declared concerning Jerusalem, “Behold, is there sorrow like My sorrow?” Therefore, “He who strikes will heal, for He Himself causes pain and then brings restoration.” For the one who takes hold is taken, whether on the sparse or on the nothing; no human can heal the wound that God inflicts. Prophecy that is vain is that which has no outcome and which fashions idols that are vain. And from themselves, some prophesied indeed, saying, “Because of the dragon of crushed barley and the fragment of bread,” according to what is written; those who do not know how to refute sin nor to rescue from the demonic captivity, through their Christology, are distorting souls. But as for the true word and the discourse which they receive from God, it is by nature true and joins to God; so too the false and elongated word of the demons, which opposes God’s inclination from there, is being driven out.

What then are the genuine outpourings, as has been shown, and the teachings? It is therefore evident that the things which expel error and lead to God are such. For 'our adversary the devil walks about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour'; and like a serpent he sends forth his poisonings against us. Yet let it not be said that he has swallowed us whole, or that he has seized upon us in the day which the burning sun accomplishes; for it has been said: 'The sun by day shall not scorch you.' For he inflames us with pleasures and wrath, and he presents error to us as light and knowledge. Therefore, as we sing, we shall say: 'If the Lord had not been in us, then surely the living would have devoured us'; and 'the lamp of the wicked shall be extinguished.' Nothing, he says, did the enemies produce of themselves; for it seemed good to God, and it came to pass. Therefore he spoke, and also Nebuzaradan: 'The Lord your God has spoken these evils against this place, and the Lord has brought it, because you have sinned against him.' Everyone therefore who disbelieves the judgment of these words shall hear it. Indeed, all the prophets foretold these things; and from ancient days Moses, in Deuteronomy, proclaimed them beforehand. There are times when the scripture causes the words to suffer, and gives sensation to the lifeless things, bringing forth leaping hills and skipping mountains, and testifying of hills and stones; which, in these things, is impossible, as the wall beneath...

title: Exalted horn versus the humble economy of Christ
english: The enemies have already been stripped bare. Therefore, here a wall is formed by the king and the rulers and all who, in power, surround this place with fortifications—those whom he deems worthy to pour out unceasing tears of repentance, tears which, to those who see them, constantly present a fallen state. These things, he says, belong to them; and if he does not again signify the sorrow of the formerly guarding power, he does so hyperbolically. “In distress,” he says, “they remembered the Lord from their whole heart.” Therefore, do this, he says: weep by night and by day, and “upon your beds, lament.” Do not regard the release from these things as sobriety; for repentance is unto salvation. Sobriety, however, belongs not to good things, but to ceasing from worse things. And let your mind be continually joined to Christ, that he may guard you as the pupil of the eye and become a wall for you. The night is watchful, as the soul is gathered within it in the stillness of the senses. Then he commands to meditate upon the commandments of God and to say with David: “By night, with my heart, I meditated; and my spirit was stirred.” And since the night is divided into four watches, say with David: “My eyes anticipated the watches,” and with Habakkuk: “I will stand upon my watch, and set myself upon the tower, and will look forth to see what he will say unto me, and what I shall answer when I am reproved.” For then you shall say: “That he will speak peace unto his people.” Therefore, meditate in silence during the night of this present age; for you do not have “a wrestling against blood and flesh, but against the principalities, against the powers.” “For you know not when the lord of the house comes, at evening, or at midnight, or at the cockcrowing, or in the morning.”

Do not suppose that the thief will come upon you unawares and find you sleeping; for if you knew at what hour the robber would come, you would have stayed awake and would not have allowed your house to be broken into. Moreover, lift up your hands to him through the work of good deeds. The struggle is not about trivial matters, but arises from the lack of understanding of the divine word, causing your little ones to falter and to stand at the beginning of all powers—the eleven commandments of God—being unable to advance without God’s cooperation and without the sustaining bread that strengthens the heart. When the prophet had exhorted, Jerusalem was persuaded and said to God: “Do not turn your face away from me,” “Look upon me and have mercy on me,” “Do not rebuke me in your anger, nor discipline me in your wrath.” The wound is greater than human nature. I know that I have transgressed the law and am subject to the ensuing penalties, among which is the statement: “You shall eat the fruit of your womb, the flesh of your sons and your daughters.” I once thought these words were merely threats, but Lord, I have come to know that “your law is truth.” Yet, as a priest and prophet, I did not learn of the slaughter taking place in the midst of the sanctuary. Upon the earth lay all those who, due to age, were unable to endure the labors—a pitiable sight, as if the slaughter of youths and virgins were not enough, and even these massacres should be led forth before entering a more bitter life. The exports of the land are the necessities of life, among which they had lain down without keeping watch or praying, having shut the eyes of the soul against sin and folly. And who are these? If they are children,

It is not at all surprising that, even now, before these events, those who seemed to have advanced in virtue and whose entire soul was blameless and capable in warfare have become subject to enemies. Yet you, as a good one, put an end to such a life for them, and you cut short every one of their establishments that is based on evil.

The ones dwelling around me in Judah, he says, who had taken refuge in me, hoping for salvation from this place—none of them remains, due to the anger you have brought upon them. For the very things by which they sinned, many and powerful enemies have now arisen against them.

Terrible things have happened to the prophet even before the city was captured and while it lay in ruins. Therefore, beginning with a different elemental instruction, he hides himself, seeing poverty and desolation in the city through the Lord’s discipline. And yet he himself has not become less in lack of good things, while at the same time having come into circumstances where he examined them, so as to say: “I spent the whole day being mocked,” and at the same time sharing in their terrible misfortunes and the sorrow that arises from compassion.

He also says, according to David: “The shadow of death has fallen upon me.” For when it seems he is giving them a brief respite from their labors, he again turns back and relentlessly pursues them, inflicting continuous punishment.

The phrase “all the day” indicates each day, as David says: “All the day fighting has oppressed me.” It would also suggest that he has turned his hand against them, and that long ago he provided me with good things, but now he brings disciplines upon me, as if he had changed his hand.
The treachery that has befallen us from sin is signified.

title: The horn cast down; rulers and the people under discipline
english: For sorrow, when it persists, induces a weakness akin to old age. For he did not allow me to escape the terrors that surround me on every side, besieging me. One might perhaps also say that the wall cast upon the city is a long, laborious burden. Yet he left me the same voice that David once uttered, saying: “He has made me sit in darkness as those who are dead of the age.” This is due both to the siege works raised against me from all sides and simultaneously to the afflictions that come from God; for the trials of the soul are darkness. Specifically, “Jeremiah was cast by Pashhur into the cistern,” a place dark and lightless, just as the cave in which David hid from Saul was dark. These two laments could also be understood as referring to Christ, of whom Jeremiah was a type, having suffered so much at the hands of the Jews and ultimately being handed over to the grave. He has clothed me in bitter things, placing upon my neck a people that is cruel and provoking, a burden heavier than what is due to me. Though I often prayed for relief, my cries were not heard; for even the prayers of the saints are sometimes hindered by circumstances. One might also liken this to the yoke and the iron chains, which God substituted for the wooden ones he had commanded, and they were placed upon me; for it is reported, and even written, that he weighed down the bronze of my neck. Indeed, he blocked my prayer and said to me: “Do not pray concerning them; for I will not hear you.” Moreover, having often been stirred to action, I was not permitted to withdraw from the burden. For he declared: “I will not name the name of the Lord,” and he was driven on as though by fire. He also obstructs the ways of the sinners, not allowing them to sin twelve times.

But such is not the prophet, who indeed says: "I did not sit in the council of those who revel." He declares that every arrow of his has been spent against me, piercing my desire and refusing to let me act as I wish. For in the Scripture, the kidneys represent the faculty of desire, and the arrows are the missiles. Moreover, they have driven me onward as a liar, having made me sing a song. And having come upon me, he said: "I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness," and what follows: the one indeed prayed for them, while the others plotted against them; yet nevertheless, the ministry was not to be declined. Thus, he prevailed and suffered all things at their hands, and he sympathized with them in their suffering, while he himself grew arrogant beneath them, acting impiously. He says, either by vote or by number, that for each tooth of the one gnashing against the cheek, there is either a hard stone. And concerning David, he says: "I ate my bread with ashes," meaning that he did not take bread with pleasure, but under affliction. Therefore, the soul could not be in peace, being troubled within and still seeing disturbances from without, and within, battles. Hence, hoping for nothing good, I have dismissed the voices of Job: "Mercy has departed from me, and my hope is from the Lord." For it was not possible to overcome the dreadful things that surround. For being good toward all, he demands our endurance. For the soul that seeks him, it is good to seek, which waits without being disturbed, until mercy answers it, and does not waver, until the saving appearance of the Lord is revealed, so that one may hope in another. Perhaps, too, he will be silent, saying that he does not meddle excessively in the providence of judgments.

It is therefore necessary, even if we are ignorant, not to neglect the Lord. For "His yoke is easy and His burden is light." Even if no one agrees with Him on this matter, we must not follow the crowd, but even if we are left alone in this stance, we must persevere and be firmly rooted in what has been decided. For the Lord says, as David declares, "He makes the solitary dwell in a house," and "I am alone until I pass over," clearly referring to those who attain the trials of philanthropy. For He humbles Himself by saying, "I am dust and ashes," if indeed He is truly a man, and the hope that does not shame is filled within Him, just as it is written, "My soul clings to the dust." This also applies to those in captivity who speak the words of the seventy-third Psalm: "Why, O God, have You cast us off forever? Why does Your anger smoke against the sheep of Your pasture?" Yet in agreement with this, it is said, "The Lord will not cast off forever, nor will He be angry to the end." And He will say to the one who has turned to worthiness: "Let your voice cease from weeping, and your eyes from tears." Through these things we learn that the Lord did not say, nor is He the cause of the humiliation of the earth's prisoners under sin, nor does He incline human judgments against God; for the Lord loves justice and uprightness, and He does not even condemn the worthy man. For He says, it is impossible for opposites to proceed from the mouth of the Lord—both good and evil. For neither does a good tree produce bad fruit, nor does a bad tree...

title: Unjust suffering under divine oversight; Israel and the enemies
english: Therefore, since we have no longer possess any other excuse but ourselves, and since we recognize that the misfortunes that befall us come from our own actions, we ought to turn back and examine the wrongs we have committed. For it is impossible to return to the Lord while remaining ignorant of oneself; yet one comes to know oneself by reflecting on one’s actions, simultaneously observing them and engaging the mind in their consideration. At that moment, with unveiled face we behold and reflect the glory of the Lord, as in a mirror, and we shall confess the things we previously acknowledged, saying: “We have sinned and we have acted lawlessly in turning away from you,” and “That you are righteous in all that you have brought upon us.” To take up the heart upon the hands seems to signify that, having taken hold of our own thoughts with our hands, we ought to examine them, if indeed they are pure. And these things constitute a part of the earlier confession: just as you, O God, brought upon us the circumstances of dreadful things by a cloud of darkness, and though we were far from you, you pursued us and destroyed the dead by means of punishment in their sins. And since our sins separate us from you, as if by a wall of cloud, our prayer did not reach you; for we did not possess “the wings of a dove” to fly upward and say, “In God I shall scale a wall.” For it was not easy to cast off sin, which is substantial, dark, and devoid of the Holy Spirit. Symmachus: destruction. With one mouth we have devoured you, and we have been brought down into the depths of evil, filled with fear and disturbance, as it is said: “He who falls into the pit which he dug,” the sinner giving the wages of what he has committed. And since, according to Solomon, “pride precedes destruction,”

This means pride—being lifted up and then shattered. That is why David sings: “Let not the foot of pride come upon me, and let the hand of the wicked not shake me.” And having endured so much from those who act arrogantly, he suffers deeply, for “love does not reckon evil.” Instead of saying my eye grew weary and would not cease from lack of vigilance, Symmachus declared: My eye endured, and it did not cease from lack of rest. The Seventy indicate that although the eyes were weakened from an abundance of tears, they did not cease, yet one could not muster the strength to resume weeping; but Symmachus says that he persisted in tears and did not cease, for a prolonged prayer and the intensity of tears draw God toward mercy. For my tears strike me, he says, like a meticulous grape gatherer striking a vine; but according to Symmachus, because the tears drowned me, using the metaphor of those who suffocate in water. Yet enduring, I will endure the Lord until He turns His face away from us. To wait for God is to hope that He will deem us worthy of His oversight. It is declared that He surpasses all in every respect—namely, upon the same afflictions—for the female nature is more compassionate than the male. Or he speaks of what he has endured: he was plunged into a pit, and as long as he remained there, he died in mind; but rescued from hope, he cried out with David: “My soul has been delivered like a bird from the snare of the fowlers,” for he was not “to fall upon the earth without the Father who is in heaven,” according to the voice of the Savior. Either he speaks of himself alone, or he also makes the sufferings of the people his own. Yet it would reasonably be said of him that he acted freely: what wrong have they done him? Rather, has he not failed to benefit them? God judged by destroying the false prophet and handing over the king, and by delivering the nation to Christ into captivity. And as for me, I—

title: Unveiled face mirroring the Lord glory
english: Their eyes were closed to me, because I was a burden to them and seemed harsh. For long before, he had said: "Bring their days to an end, and your word will be to me a joy and gladness of heart." All this happened after the plot against the Savior, when they were scattered everywhere; for he came upon them, saying, "Every righteous blood poured out." The completion of this act shows that they received the full measure of the worship due against them, and that they no longer enriched the people of God. The defense of my heart was a labor to them, because you will give them toil as a sensation of how long you have been defending them, so that they may seek you again. But if not, you will pursue them in your wrath. Beginning the present fourth elementary instruction, he took up again the lament concerning the eminent ones, saying that the surface was to be darkened, declaring that the justice poured out like water had been wiped away. Yet the holy ones, as elect through the fathers or through those taken with Joachim, whom he likened to good figs. And shortly after: from the departures of those from the holy land, "leading them to destruction," and into the intellectual Babylon, "that they may be taught not to blaspheme." You might say the lament also applies to those who change from godliness, if indeed they are notable and lead others into error, "having left the fountain of living water, become cracked cisterns that cannot hold." Therefore, they pour out about the error, groaning early. The fourteen who adorn themselves with wealth, or even with gold more precious, how could they thus be brought low against the humble and broken, led into slavery, and be imagined as such? Yet he said to them that they should imagine themselves, and when he went down "to the potter's house," having taken a vessel, he broke it.

Origen continues his lament over the ruined state of Jerusalem, citing Isaiah’s prophecy that the city’s ruins would be like shattered pottery—worthless fragments of a broken vessel. He then turns to the famine that struck the noble citizens, describing how even infants suffered, so extreme was the deprivation that Jerusalem, once a mother to its people, could no longer provide nourishment—not even to beasts in the field, let alone to its own children. This overwhelming suffering and the resulting forgetfulness of human nature, he says, work together to produce a spiritual desolation. In this state, people begin to heed the whispers of evil spirits, likened to dragons or the Sirens as understood by Symmachus, whose seductive voices lead them astray. These evil influences are those who have introduced the teachings of the impious, corrupting the young with false doctrine. Origen asks rhetorically: how can those who have been made effeminate by such teachings—whom even Pharaoh once sought to destroy by killing the males—still be considered daughters? They have abandoned the true teaching of God, the desert wisdom, and instead wander the earth, feeding on falsehoods like ostriches that cannot fly. Symmachus, in his translation, used the term “ostrich” to describe such useless teachers, and Origen agrees, noting that just as the Sirens of myth lured travelers to destruction with sweet sounds, so too do these false teachers ensnare the innocent with pleasing but deadly words. He rebukes even the good teachers among them, saying they have not shown equal concern for those who wander in search of truth. These trials—of siege and exile—have been endured by the people. One might say, as the prophetic word declares, that they suffered famine not for lack of bread or water, but because they were deprived of hearing the word of the Lord. Therefore, Origen prophesies concerning their newborns, who inherit this spiritual barrenness. Historically, he reflects on the events of the captivity, but intellectually he turns to the famine of the teaching word—the absence of true doctrine. For, he insists, the poverty of those who suffer is not so much in material lack as in this deeper, more grievous spiritual destitution.

For these also Paul laments, saying, "Whose is the adoption and the glory." For now they engage in empty studies, not delighting in Moses and the prophets, as in the command, "Beat your breast for the Lord." Indeed, none of them breaks to them the nourishing word, nor do they partake of the fattened calf, though they themselves have sacrificed. He calls the dispersions "exoduses," or also the deviations of the legal writings. Formerly they were fed on the scarlet dye, they prophetically heard the future outpouring of the Savior’s blood, and now they tear themselves apart from earthly thoughts. Symmachus says the one, as if in haste, suddenly gave forth; the other, they did not labor, which they did not wound. For what more concise word of God has said, "Behold, your house is left to you desolate," and only to him who is willing to give? The lawlessness of Jerusalem has been magnified above that of Sodom. Those had only the natural law; these also had the written law and the prophets, as many marvelous things God worked in them. Those indeed erred toward angels and like men; but these toward the Savior and Redeemer long ago, indeed from Egypt, now to the worship of demons, if they received the One who came to them beforehand. title: Glory reflected, the letter withdrawn, and the spirit sight
english: More fiery in nature than the things visible to the eye, sapphire are their limbs, their appearance darker than soot. Those who sanctified themselves to God, he says, are made holy—indeed, the term Nazirites conveys this, as Symmachus and Theodotion likewise rendered the sanctified in Amos as Nazirites. Moses also remembers these, of what sort he was, and even Samson. They were also prominent among the Judeans. Therefore, their purity was tested against snow, their brightness against milk; yet they were refined by ascetic discipline, having been proven in what they had promised to God. But the elect among them—this is indicated by the fragment—possess a heavenly commonwealth, for such is the color of sapphire. Moreover, they have golden veins, by which Symmachus represents their constitution, possessing incorruptibility and enduring fire through piety. From the spiritual radiance they have fallen, weakened by intellectual hunger, so as to resemble dry wood, like those not planted by the watercourses; such are now the priests among them, possessing no spiritual nourishment. And according to the explicit statement, their faces have grown blackened from utter shame, because, though sinning like others, they were led away; and even now, the custom among those being disgraced is to use the name in this way. For in war, it is better to die swiftly than to be subdued by famine due to lack of field produce. One might even say the sword and the dagger are the word of God—for Paul says: “and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God”—by whom,

The bride says, "I am wounded by love." And David also says, "Gird your sword upon your thigh, mighty one, in your splendor and your beauty." Those struck by such swords—spears of divine judgment—it is fitting that they fall beneath Jesus’ feet, as it is written: "The peoples shall fall under you." They have confessed his kingdom, yet they are not to be destroyed by spiritual famine. For Christ is the offspring of a land, he who was born in Bethlehem, which is called "House of Bread." The Jews, having become estranged from this bread, have been driven away into the land of demons. But the field blessed by the Lord, exceedingly fragrant, which Jacob breathed upon, signifies the Church of Christ. 105 Lest the women think they have eaten their children through cruelty, he says they are compassionate; yet he attributes this to the necessity of scarcity. The act of kindling and roasting indicates what came to pass during the Roman siege; therefore, he calls the complete destruction of the nation a shattering. And in the second chapter of Lamentations, he treats the present suffering as an element of sorrow. And this, along with all other passions, Josephus has transmitted with accuracy in his writings on the siege. 106 For after the coming of Christ, these things were completed. 107 Perhaps indeed because of the strength of the place, the fortress, and the strength of its inhabitants, but most of all because of the God who continually protects the city. Yet before Nebuchadnezzar entered, the Egyptian often took the treasures from the house of the Lord, but did not destroy the city; for he did not greatly oppress it, even if he was an enemy.

Origen reflects on the paradoxical nature of divine wisdom, noting how the rulers of the earth and the demonic powers that once governed the nations—those referenced in Scripture as having gathered together against the Lord and His Christ—acted in ignorance. Had they understood the true identity of the Lord of glory, they would not have crucified Him. Their lack of knowledge stemmed from a mistaken belief that Jerusalem would not ultimately fall, as they clung to the idea that God’s promise to the patriarchs would be fulfilled in their time, unaware of the deeper mystery surrounding Christ. Yet it is precisely the righteous blood of Christ the Savior, poured out completely, that those who shed it ultimately destroyed themselves, even as they attempted to find moderation by comparing their guilt to the blood of the prophets. Symmachus describes the aftermath: they became unstable, blind in their ways, covered in blood to such an extent that they could not even touch their own garments. Meanwhile, Scripture calls the angels “watchers,” as seen in Daniel, and it is possible that the law given through Moses was mediated by such beings, as suggested by the phrase “if the law spoken through angels was…” Those who persisted in clinging to the law and the temple, despite being shaken by these events, were eventually displaced. title: From affliction to contemplation with unveiled face
english:
Let us go from here.
At the time when, according to Symmachus, they became unstable and wandering and blind, he says, in their exits.
For it is not "a vision that separates";
nor is it king, nor prophet, nor leader; for "they have failed" because "he came to whom they were looking forward, who was the expectation of the nations."
To the apostles he commands to flee from among the Jews upon the blood of Christ having been defiled, but he permits their calling and also to the angels.
If not, then he would be commanding the apostles to call the unclean to repentance, which they did, saying: "It was necessary for you first to speak the word."
But if they are unwilling, he commands them to flee; therefore they say, as if unwilling, "Behold, we turn to the Gentiles."
And it indicates that the one was lifted up—the fire of the destruction; the other was shaken—the migration into slavery; and the third will not add to dwelling here, because they will have permanent dwelling, no longer needing second things.
He indicates the punishment from Christ: for David says, "The face of the Lord is upon those doing evil."
They do not look upon him, remaining as they are; for "when the fullness of the Gentiles has entered, all Israel will be saved," and afterward he looks upon them as faithful.
But if it were written: a part of them, it is clear that he speaks of those going out from the midst.
Concerning the enemies, the face of the priests they did not take, for he led them all away.
From the captives, the word seems to be, of those repenting concerning the Egyptians and Assyrians to whom they gave aid.
And it could be said, consistently, by those who believed from circumcision: they left the empty hope in the law, expecting.

For the law saves no one, as the apostle Paul has said. Therefore, those who cling to the law will not be able to help after grace has come. Under the Savior, those who were made fishermen of men—the disciples—went out hunting Jews with the nets of their minds, so that they would not walk upon the broad and spacious way of their fathers. Thus, even as the Savior himself inclined himself, saying, "Allow the children to come to me." For Josephus records that not even the mountains saved those who fled. There, therefore, as they dragged us, they seized us, or rather, they brought us before judgment against us. Let it be considered also concerning the apostles, of whom it was said, "Their youth was renewed like that of an eagle." Some have said that in the chosen ones, Josiah mourns more clearly, for they hoped that through his piety, Jerusalem would rise again in the midst of the nations for glory, since Jerusalem is in the midst of the nations. And this, they say, is a type of Christ, who died because of the lawlessness of the people. Yet he was not seized among the corruptions of the people, but as one who met the king of Egypt, Necho, after the prophet had forbidden it, even though he was unwilling to fight against him. Therefore, according to the divine apostle: "A veil lies upon the face of the Jews when Moses is read; but when one turns to the Lord, the veil is taken away, and the Lord is the Spirit." And through the prophet, the Lord is spoken of as the rational Spirit. Those upon whom the veil lies would not, if they could, say that Christ is the Spirit of our face, but rather, "we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from glory to glory," and the Lord is ever before the eyes of our mind.

It is evident that the active force present in the prophets was the Spirit of Christ, who, having become incarnate, declares: “I myself, the one who speaks, am here.” He is the Spirit, the Lord, and the Christ. Those who corrupted the divine seed within themselves first seized him. But we, the prophets, do not regard another as the Spirit of our person; after our conception, we no longer possess a place among them. Instead, we live under the shadow of Christ, no longer among the Jews, but among all the nations, at the time when “the kingdom of God was taken from them” because of their boldness against Christ, and “it was given to the nations.” Behold, the prophets now live within us, speaking about him and proclaiming him, yet no longer among those who still, even now, envelop him in their own corruptions, blaspheming him day by day. Aquilas said that the Spirit is the breath of our nostrils; Symmachus said it is the breath of our nostrils. For the God-loving continually breathe in Christ, having him before their eyes. Know this: just as Christ, being Spirit, spoke in the prophets, so also the Father speaks; for Paul says in the letter to the Hebrews: “Long ago, God spoke in many and varied ways to our ancestors through the prophets, but in these last days he has spoken to us by his Son.” And so too the Holy Spirit: for the Savior says, “Well did the Holy Spirit speak through Isaiah: ‘You will indeed hear but never understand…’”

title: One Spirit distributing gifts; prophecy among the charisms
english: You were told. Moreover, in the First Epistle to the Corinthians, when Paul speaks of the spiritual gifts—among which is prophecy—he says: "All these things are energized by one and the same Spirit, who distributes to each individually as He wills." This means authoritatively, not servilely. One might say that the Spirit is the person of Christ, the One who bestowed upon us the Spirit of prophecy; for this very Spirit of prophecy is the person of the prophets, while the Spirit itself is the gift, and the Law is but a shadow—since "the Law has a shadow of the good things to come." Thus, the prophets lived within us and within the shadow of the Law. Therefore, the prophetic gift, toward which every manifestation of prophecy looks as its goal, is Christ, that is, from Christ. For "Christ is the end of the Law and the prophets." Moreover, it could be said even from the person of the apostles and the believers: "For in Him we live and move and have our being"—of whom we said that we would live in His shadow.

title: Become imitators; the word against Edom and Esau hatred
english: This is to say, according to his imitation. For the divine apostle says, "Be imitators of me, as I also am of Christ." This word is directed to those from Edom and Esau, the brother of Jacob, proclaiming to them an excess of evils (for this is what the drunken one will pour out and drain), concerning which David also says: "Remember, Lord, the sons of Edom on the day of Jerusalem, of those saying, 'Strip her bare, strip her bare, until her foundation is laid bare.'" For being brothers and neighbors, they have preserved the ancestral hatred. And concerning Christ, having spoken, he remembered this at the opportune time. For the Christ was about to destroy the earthly one, so named, working heavenly things. For virtue and knowledge are threatening.

title: All Israel saved; the Church as daughter of the synagogue
english: It will be saved after the full number of the Gentiles has come in, having abandoned lawlessness; then the consummation will follow, and the punishment of earthly things, as we await the judgment. Indeed, the word might also be spoken to the church, which is the daughter of the ancient synagogue, for “the gifts of God are irrevocable,” yet its lawlessness has departed through divine baptism; she whom the Speaker no longer hands over to the enemies says, “Here I will dwell, for I have chosen her,” and “Behold, I am with you always, to the end of the age,” when even impiety was established among those who mind earthly things.
